articles.author: Azir
articles.description:
I’ve spent years building websites and small platforms where booking functionality was needed.
Over time, I realized I was either rebuilding the same foundations again and again or relying on hosted platforms and plugin-heavy CMS setups that I didn’t fully control.
So I decided to build a self-hosted booking and website system that I could actually own, extend, and reuse across projects.
Some deliberate choices I made:

• No plugin-based architecture

• Full control over data and hosting

• Modular structure that can grow beyond a single use case  
It started as an internal tool for accommodation websites and slowly evolved into a production-ready system.
I’m curious how other developers here approach similar problems:
I’m also curious how other developers here approach sharing or distributing similar self-hosted tools — especially when they’re not SaaS products.
If anyone is curious, the system I built for this is called BellaVista.
You can find more details here:
https://bellavistaproject.eu
Looking forward to hearing your thoughts.
articles.title: Why I built a self-hosted booking platform instead of using SaaS tools

When something breaks in production, reproducing it locally means wrestling with event structures and Lambda-specific context objects.

articles.author: Kervie Sazon
articles.description:
This post summarizes what I have learned about the most common Linux directories and how they are used in a typical system.
/ - Root Directory
/bin - Binaries
ls
cd
cp
mv
rm 
/dev - Device Files
/dev/null

This line of code can be sent to destroy any file or string.
/dev/zero

This line of code contains an infinite sequence of 0.
/dev/random

This line of code contains an infinite sequence of random values.
/etc - Configuration Files
/usr - User System Resources
/usr/bin - contains basic user commands.
‘/usr/sbin’ - contains additional commands for the administrator.
‘/usr/lib’ - contains the system libraries.
/usr/share’ - contains documentation manual pages. 
/home - User Home Directories
/home/Downloads

/lib - Shared Libraries
These directories store shared libraries required by system binaries in /bin and /sbin.
They are essential for the system to boot and function properly.
articles.title: Linux Fundamentals - Part 2: Understanding Directory Hierarchy

articles.author: Anthony Narcise
articles.description:
The Hook


Most developer tools are built to be "safe." They have clean lines, predictable buttons, and a sense of order. At @AvyroxSolutions, we decided to do the opposite. We built Vokrix—a GitHub analyzer that doesn't just roast your code; it tries to break your reality.
The Vision: Atmospheric Engineering


We wanted to move beyond the "SaaS dashboard" aesthetic. By implementing a Dynamic Theme & Localized Identity engine, we created a platform that shifts based on "Moods".
Hacker Mode: High-contrast terminal green with mechanical keyboard haptics.
Chaos Mode: A violent red theme that triggers a "Reality Breach" using horizontal screen tearing and VHS scanlines.
The Technical Deep Dive: The "Melt" and the "Breach"


To make the CHAOS mode feel visceral, we used a combination of:
SVG Gooey Filters: We used feGaussianBlur and feColorMatrix to make the logo literally "bleed" and melt when the system enters a critical state.
State-Driven Soundscapes: We synced industrial hums and digital whines to the generation logic to create sensory overload.
The Hidden Command: We implemented a global listener for a specific keyboard sequence—"BREAK"—which triggers a simulated kernel panic and reveals a hidden technical cheat sheet.
Why Psychological UX Matters


As engineers at Avyrox Solutions, we believe the best way to prove you can handle a client's complex infrastructure is to show you have absolute control over your own UI. If we can safely simulate a "system failure" that scares the user, imagine what we can do for your actual uptime.
The Challenge


I’ve opened a private beta for the next 24 hours. I want to see if you can find the backdoor and "break" the system to unlock our internal architecture docs.
Try it here: https://vokrix.app
Check out the team behind it: https://avyrox-solutions.com
Discussion for the Comments



How do you feel about "hostile" UI design for marketing?
What’s the coolest SVG filter trick you’ve seen lately?
Did you find the BREAK command? (No spoilers!)
articles.title: Why I Built a GitHub Roaster That "Melts" Your Browser (And How I Did It)

Making Date-Based Content Reusable



  
  
  Problem


Content with specific dates can't be reused.
Example: An exam with these dates:
Grading due: Jan 18, 2024
Appeal deadline: Jan 20, 2024
Confirmation due: Jan 22, 2024
Want to reuse this exam in July? You have to manually update every date.

exam.grade_due = datetime(2024, 1, 18)

Can't reuse
Every instance needs manual date updates
2. Copy everything
july_exam = copy(jan_exam)
july_exam.grade_due = datetime(2024, 7, 18)
# Update 10+ date fields...

Content duplication
Update original? Copies don't change
Maintenance nightmare
3. Templates with placeholders
exam.dates = "{{start_date}} + 3 days"

Complex parsing
No type safety
Hard to query
Content layer: Relative dates (…

Two months ago, our internal knowledge base chatbot confidently told a support rep that our refund policy was “14 days, no questions asked.” Our real policy is 30 days with approval for larger amounts.
A $2,000 refund was processed based on that hallucination.
That was the moment we stopped treating LLM features like “smart text boxes” and started treating them like unreliable distributed systems that require real engineering.
This article is not about demos. It’s about what you have to build after the demo works.
Traditional backends are deterministic.
Same input → same output.
AI backends are probabilistic.
Same input → slightly different output depending on context, model variance, and prompt structure.
This means:
You cannot trust outputs
You cannot trust retrieval
You cannot trust pro…
